opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's funny, because vision is one of those areas where the models can look superhuman one moment and then completely fall over on something a five-year-old would get right. You'll give it a dense chart or a messy screenshot, and it'll pull out details you didn't even notice. Then you ask it to count the objects in a simple image, or tell you which line is longer, or read an analog clock, and it just confidently gets it wrong.

A lot of that, I think, comes down to how perception and reasoning are glued together. The model sees an image through some compressed representation, and then most of the "thinking" happens in language. So if the fine-grained spatial information didn't survive that step, no amount of clever reasoning afterward will recover it. The model will happily reason its way to a wrong answer because it was working from a slightly blurry picture in its head.

The other tricky part is evaluation. With text you can often check whether the reasoning chain makes sense. With images it's harder to tell whether the model actually *looked* at the thing or just pattern-matched to what images like that usually contain. We've seen cases where it describes what should be in a picture rather than what is in it, and that's subtle and hard to catch at scale.

What I'm most excited about is getting models to interact with images more actively: zooming in, cropping, going back and re-examining a region when they're uncertain, the way a person would squint at something. That loop of perceiving, reasoning, and then looking again seems really important, and we're only starting to scratch the surface of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that's tricky is that vision looks solved from a distance and then falls apart the moment you ask the model to actually do something with what it sees. Captioning an image, telling you there's a dog on a couch, that's basically done. But if you hand it a dense chart and ask what the value was in Q3 of 2019, or you give it a screenshot and ask it to click the third button from the left, suddenly you're in a very different regime. You need the model to localize precisely, to read small text, to count, to reason about spatial relationships, and those are exactly the things that the standard pretraining recipe doesn't give you for free.

Part of the problem is just data. The internet has an enormous amount of text where people explain their reasoning, but there's very little natural data where someone looks at an image and narrates, step by step, how they figured out what's in it. So the model learns to recognize things but not to perceive carefully. It'll glance at a problem, pattern-match to something plausible, and commit. And when it's wrong it's confidently wrong, because there's no internal signal telling it that it should look again.

Another thing we think about a lot is resolution and tokenization. How many tokens do you spend on an image? If you downsample aggressively, the model's fast and cheap but it literally cannot see the fine detail you're asking about. If you go high resolution, you're burning context on mostly uninformative pixels. So there's a real tradeoff there, and the right answer depends on the task, which the model doesn't necessarily know in advance.

And then evaluation is genuinely hard. A lot of the public vision benchmarks are either saturated or contaminated, or they test something fairly shallow. We've found that we have to build evals that are much closer to the real use cases, things like reading diagrams, or multi-step visual reasoning, or operating a computer, because improvements on the standard benchmarks don't always translate. You can get a few points on a leaderboard and have the model still fail at what people actually want it to do.

So I'd say the honest summary is that the model is great at seeing in the loose sense and still pretty unreliable at looking in the careful sense. Closing that gap is a lot of what we're working on.

astra-6.text: I think the tricky part is telling whether the model actually understands what it’s seeing. It can give you a very convincing description of an image, but then you ask a precise question—how many objects are there, or how are they positioned relative to one another—and it can struggle. So there’s this gap between being able to talk about an image fluently and being able to reliably reason about the details. And the fluency makes that gap surprisingly hard to spot.

r001.rationale: The response discusses difficulty with precise visual questions generally, but does not mention the models answering 10:10 when asked to read a clock.

sol-6.1.text: The tricky thing is that visual understanding isn’t one capability. A model can describe an image really well and still struggle with a basic question about where something is or how many objects are there. So you get this gap between how convincing the answer sounds and how precisely the model understands the scene. And that makes evaluation hard: are we measuring what it actually sees, or what it can plausibly infer from context?
